summary: Carysfort Reef's 1852 iron screw-pile tower off Key Largo: lit for over a century, deactivated in 2014 as unsafe, offered at a 2022 federal auction.

light.characteristic: Three flashes in a group from a screened first-order lens (Bulletin 1931); flashing white with three red sectors from 30 April 1893 (Board list)

lens.where: Original first-order revolving lens, July 1852 (nomination). Replaced by a third-order lens in 1962; a modern beacon from 1982.

structures.type: octagonal pyramidal iron skeleton on nine screw piles
structures.note: 100 ft to the lantern (USLHS); focal plane 106 ft above mean low water (nomination); GSA gives a 124-ft tower

structures.type: two-story iron house in the form of a truncated cone, within the tower's base

staffing.note: Last resident keepers left in 1962 (LighthouseFriends). The 1984 nomination says the light was de-manned after the Second World War.

access.note: Not open to the public (USLHS). Deactivated by the Coast Guard in 2014 as unstable and unsafe; about six miles offshore inside the sanctuary (GSA).

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard until its 2019 excess declaration; GSA online auction 2022 (top bid $415,000; buyer and closing not confirmed in the sources read)

events.note: Congress provided $20,000 for a lightship on the reef (LighthouseFriends)
Lightship Caesar on station; this is the 1825 date in the record. It is a lightship, not the tower.
Replacement lightship (Florida) funded after the Caesar's dry rot (LighthouseFriends)
On 26 June 1837 the Florida's keeper, John Whalton, and one of his men were shot dead by Seminoles after landing on Key Largo (LighthouseFriends quoting a crew member)
Congress provided $20,000 for a lighthouse to replace the lightship; another $40,000 followed in 1838 (LighthouseFriends)
Iron skeleton tower and keepers' house completed; the 1937 Bulletin says the tower was begun to replace the lightship
First illuminated 10 March 1852 as a fixed light (nomination)
First-order revolving Fresnel lens made in Paris by Henry Lepaute, July 1852 (nomination; USLHS gives 1852). LighthouseFriends gives 1855 for the lens.
Changed from flashing white to flashing white with three red sectors, 30 April 1893
New machinery to replace the revolving machinery of the light (Board report)
Oil house (concrete, 13 by 15 feet) completed for $188, fiscal 1916-17
Keeper William H. Curry drowned in the September 1919 hurricane (Bulletin 1919; LighthouseFriends)
Keepers Charles F. Fine and Eley J. Whidden rescued the motor yacht Napinee, 4 January 1922 (Commissioner's report; LighthouseFriends)
Switched to electricity in 1926; lower level of tower partly enclosed for a generator (nomination)
Storm reported in the 1926 Bulletin: one small boat washed away at Carysfort Reef, minor damage (the bulletin gives no date within the year)
Hurricane took the spiral stair; replaced with a wood ladder (nomination)
Bulletin of 1931 describes the three-flash group from a first-order lens with every fourth flash panel replaced by a metal screen (the change date is not given)
Last resident keepers left; Coast Guard automated the light (LighthouseFriends)
Fixed third-order lens replaced the revolving first-order lens (LighthouseFriends)
Hurricane Donna destroyed the iron balcony around the keepers' house; iron cresting on the tower destroyed in the 1966 hurricane (nomination)
Third-order lens removed when a modern beacon was placed in the tower (LighthouseFriends)
National Register reference 84000199; the nomination is signed July 1984
Coast Guard deactivated the light after finding the structure unstable and considered unsafe; the light's flashing is now shown from a nearby structure forty feet high (LighthouseFriends)
Declared excess to Coast Guard needs on 1 February 2019; no qualified organization took it over (LighthouseFriends)
GSA online auction; bidding closed 16 May 2022 with a top bid of $415,000. Buyer and closing not confirmed in the sources read.

corrections.why: The tower was built 1848-1852 and first lit 10 March 1852 (nomination; USLHS 'Year Tower Established: 1852'; Bulletin 1937). The 1825 date belongs to the lightship Caesar.
The light was first illuminated on 10 March 1852 (nomination). The USLHS 'Year Established: 1825' refers to the station's lightship; the record's 1825 is that lightship.

notes_for_editor: (1) Lens history conflicts. The nomination: fixed light lit 10 March 1852, first-order revolving Fresnel by Henry Lepaute in July 1852. USLHS: first-order Fresnel installed 1852. LighthouseFriends: lamps first, a first-order Fresnel replaced them in 1855, and it was activated 17 March 1858 when Sombrero Key was lit. The story follows the nomination. (2) Engineer's name: LighthouseFriends gives Major Thomas B. Linnard; the nomination gives Thomas E. Lannard. The story uses Linnard and notes the spelling. Check a primary source. (3) Dates for automation: the nomination says de-manned after the Second World War; LighthouseFriends and the roster (keepers to 1962) put the last resident keepers in 1962. The story uses 1962. (4) Height: USLHS 100 ft (to the lantern, above mean high water); nomination focal plane 106 ft above mean low water; GSA 124-ft tower; LighthouseFriends 'forty feet' for the present flashing structure. The record's 30.5 m is left as it is. (5) Distance: the nomination places the reef '12 miles northeast of South Channel, Key Largo'; GSA and LighthouseFriends say about six miles off Key Largo. The story uses six miles (GSA). (6) The record's 2014 'built (Tower 2)' is not supported by any source read. The 2014 entry in LighthouseFriends is the deactivation, and the flashing is now from a structure at forty feet, of unstated date. Not corrected here; check the structure's date. (7) WWII lookout use (nomination): the nomination gives no year, so no year is entered in events. (8) The 1926 storm (Bulletin 1926) gives no date within that year; the event uses the publication year. (9) The 1931 characteristic change (Bulletin 1931): the change date is not given; the event uses the year of the bulletin. (10) The sale: Keys News says the winning bidder had until 30 June 2022 to complete; no source read names the buyer or confirms a closing. (11) The roster: 196 lines; 34 head keepers; 20 Coast Guard lines (1959-1962) normalised to role 'other' with a USCG note; the 'Assistant Keeper (rank unknown)' line is normalised to 'assistant'. Shared person slugs are the USLHS's. (12) Keeper name variance: the Bulletin index 1918-1923 spells 'Chester F. Fine' where the roster, LighthouseFriends and the 1922 bulletin give Charles F. Fine. The story follows the roster. (13) The Brookfield anecdote (LighthouseFriends) is undated; Jenks's keepership (1928-1939) is the only date in the page's dialogue. Presented as a recollection. (14) The Service's 1925-1927 bulletin entries and the 1918-1923 index entries (keeper drowns, p.97; keepers tow yacht, p.219) are the index's own entries and were not cited because the index PDF is not in the local corpus; the 1919 bulletin (p.41) is cited for the Curry death. (15) A Service retirement notice in the 1927 bulletin (p.8) names a keeper who began at Carysfort Reef in 1899; the name is not legible in the OCR and was not used. (16) Boat drift and the Napinee: the Commissioner's report calls the Napinee a motor boat; the bulletins and LighthouseFriends call it a motor yacht; the story says motor yacht. (17) The 1837 killings are a lightship-era event: lightship keepers are not in this roster. (18) The Carysfort Reef Lighthouse Foundation is an advocacy group; its claim that the structure is deteriorating is cited as its own statement. (19) No newspaper sources were used. (20) The NHLPA report (npshistory.com) gives 124+ ft; not used. (21) No photos were added. (22) The record's 'Fl Y 4s' characteristic and the 1825 'built' and first_lit dates are corrected in the corrections block; the 2014 'Tower 2' is flagged in note 6. (23) The 1926 bulletin's 90 mph is the highest wind estimated at Carysfort Reef; a 125 mph figure in the same report is for another station and is not used. (24) The 1896-97 and 1900 Board volumes: scan page = position in the volume, counted from 0; printed page read from the page head (117 in both). The 1896 and 1900 page numbers were wrong before this check (65 and 139 in the story's earlier footnotes; now 372 and 138). (25) Dates for the lens: LighthouseFriends gives 1855 for the Fresnel lens and 17 March 1858 for the revolving activation; the nomination gives July 1852. Both are stated in the story. (26) First of the later appropriations: 1847 (LighthouseFriends) vs design started 1848 (nomination); both stated. (27) The roster has 196 lines, one per stint, not 196 people. (28) The story's Brookfield anecdote is LighthouseFriends' own account of a recollection, stated as such; the source gives no date, so none is given.
